en: *Sammitīya-nikāya-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
Homage to the All-Knowing One! From this discourse: Thus it is. When such a person is on the verge of death,
When one achieves a mind of indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-citta*), by what karma is one reborn?
The answer is:

there is karma where the indeterminate mind is accompanied by delusion, and through such karmic afflictions one goes to the evil realms; there is karma where the indeterminate mind is free from delusion, and through pure karma (*śukla-karman*) one goes to the good realms.
The nature of the mind is indeterminate; for this reason, one acts in accordance with it.
By means of an indeterminate mind, one gives rise to indeterminate karma, and because of the constraints of that karma, one is reborn accordingly.
It is thus.
Therefore, there is no interruption in the activity; whether one is asleep, fainting, or dies in a state of unconsciousness, because the activity is restrained, one proceeds to the path of karma.
These first two segments of discourse reveal association, while the third segment reveals non-loss: that karma is one's own doing, one's own karma.
What is the meaning of "self-made"?
Answer: It has the sense of "experiencing."
What is the meaning of "one's own karma" (*svakarma*)? Answer:
It means "a portion."
Why is this? Because it does not go elsewhere. Why is this arising [so]?
Because it is a skillful means.
Why is this the sphere of practice?
Because it is due to that.
This is not extinguished. Why? Because of sensation, because of this manifestation, and because the karma performed in this world is not extinguished.
Through the ripening of karma, one undergoes birth in the four states of existence.

In this case, one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm; there are places where one goes into the intermediate state, and there are places where one undergoes the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). It is thus:
whether in a location of the desire realm or a location of the form realm—namely, the first and third locations—an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) may be so described.
Thus it is.

From the intermediate existence of the desire realm, one undergoes the intermediate existence of the desire realm; from the intermediate existence of the desire realm, one undergoes the intermediate existence of the form realm.
Thus it is.
This is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) between death and rebirth in this desire realm;
it is thus, thus.
As for the third case: from an intermediate existence of the form realm, one undergoes an intermediate existence of the form realm; in this same way, we die and undergo an intermediate existence.
It is so. How is it that the World-Honored One’s śrāvakas receive an intermediate existence from an intermediate existence, yet are not ordinary worldlings? Why is this so?

Because the srotāpanna, having seven more births and seven more deaths from here, receives an intermediate existence in the heavens; dwelling there, he realizes the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin. This is how it is.

Those who, from an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the heavens, receive an intermediate existence among humans and dwell here, cultivate revulsion toward the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and realize this [fruit].

Those who, from an intermediate existence among humans, receive an intermediate existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and dwell in that intermediate state, attain parinirvāṇa on the spot; they constitute one type of "one-interval" practitioner (*ekavīcika*). From there, they enter another intermediate existence and attain parinirvāṇa at that location.
In this way, the śrāvaka transcends four intermediate existences (*antarābhava*).

There are certain schools that say: "Once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) already [transcend them]; for a once-returner, in the state of an intermediate existence, they reach the stage of 'one-interval' (*ekavīcika*), thereby crossing over the intermediate existence."
It is so; it is so. From the desire realm heavens one receives [birth] in the desire realm heavens; thus it should be understood.
There are those who abandon the five aggregates of the place of birth-existence and receive the five aggregates of the intermediate existence; all such cases are like this.
From this point forward, I shall now speak: how does the self exist?
How is it that one abandons this existence and takes up another existence?
It is asked:
What is the cause of your doubt? He replied:
"I have seen that the intentions of my former teachers were mutually contradictory; therefore, doubt has arisen."
Certain schools maintain that there is no real self, and that the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas) alone constitute the self. Why is this?
Because suffering merely arises.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said to Kātyāyana:
"Only suffering arises; only suffering ceases.
He merely perceives the arising of suffering; thus, one knows that the various schools perceive that there is no self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that there is no self? Answer:
Because there is no such teaching, the World-Honored One further said to the brahmin Śreṇika:
"Regarding the Dharma as you perceive it, speak truthfully that there is no self."
The World-Honored One said:
"One who sees in this way is called a teacher; he is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—this is what I have taught."
Because those various schools do not teach [a self], there is therefore no self;
it is thus.
Furthermore, in what sense is "no-self" taught?
Answer: Because one sees one's own body.
The World-Honored One said:
Ignorant worldlings, lacking learning and wisdom, perceive form as the self, the self as possessing form, form as being within the self, and the self as being within form.
These four modes apply likewise to the other four aggregates.
If there were a self, one would not abandon the view of one's own body and instead take the five aggregates as its essence.

It would be like a person who abandons his own body and takes Devadatta’s body as the view of his own body; that body would be Devadatta, Devadatta would be within that body, and that body would be within Devadatta.

For example, if one were to discard the faculty of the eye and take the "seeing by Devadatta" or the "seeing by ivory" as one's own knowledge and vision, it would not be his seeing; therefore, there is no self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, in what sense is it said that there is no self? Answer:
Because "self" and "what belongs to self" cannot be apprehended.
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"If there were a self, then there would be what belongs to self; if there were what belongs to self, then there would be a self."
The self and what belongs to the self cannot be found as ultimate reality; therefore, there is no self.
Because those various schools see that the self and what belongs to the self cannot be found, they maintain that there is thus no self.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that there is no self?
Answer: Because one falsely claims that which is unreal exists.
As Pūrṇa said to the bhikṣus: "Venerable ones!
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is exceedingly difficult to fathom; within the absence of any entity, there is a self."
The Buddha himself said: "I, too, Elder, am like this."
I only know these words; I cannot fathom their profound meaning in this way.
Because it is said that [the self] exists as something unreal, and because one knows that the views of the various schools concern unreal meanings, therefore there is no self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, various schools maintain that one cannot say there is a self, nor can one say there is no self. Why is this?
Answer: Because the mark of a self (ātman) is inexpressible. Answer:

One who possesses a self can be described, just as a conditioned phenomenon can be described by its characteristic of being conditioned, or as the unconditioned can be described by its characteristic of being unconditioned; likewise, a self can be described by its characteristic of being a self.
Because those various schools see that the characteristic of a self (*ātman*) is inexpressible, they maintain that both "there is a self" and "there is no self" are inexpressible.
It is thus.
Furthermore, for what reason are "there is a self" and "there is no self" inexpressible?
Answer: Because it is answered by setting the question aside. Why is this so?
There are four ways of answering questions:

first, answering directly upon being asked; second, answering after first posing a counter-objection; third, answering by means of a counter-question; and fourth, setting the question aside without answering.
Now, when you question me, I simply set it aside and do not record [an answer]; therefore, one cannot say that there is a self, nor can one say that there is no self.
It is thus.
Furthermore, for what reason are "self" and "no-self" unspeakable?
Answer: Because of their fixed distinction and conjunction.
If there were a self, it should be possible to say whether it is identical to the formations or distinct from them.
Is this conditioned or unconditioned?
Since these two explanations are both indeterminate, it cannot be said that there is a self, nor can it be said that there is no self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that "self" and "non-self" are inexpressible? Answer:
Because permanence and impermanence are conjoined.
If a self could be spoken of, would it be permanent or impermanent?
One of these two positions must necessarily be determinate; yet it is not determinate. Therefore, one cannot say that there is a self, nor can one say that there is no self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason are "self" and "non-self" inexpressible?
Answer:
Because they rely upon existence and non-existence, the Buddha told Kātyāyana:
"The world relies on two things; it relies both on existence and on non-existence. For this reason, it clings to existence and clings to non-existence."
Therefore, it is thus: it cannot be said whether there is a self or no self.
Furthermore, various schools maintain that a real self exists.
Why is this? Because of the bondage of speech.
The Buddha said:
These are the fetters of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, by which one crosses from this world to that.
Because those various schools maintain that the view of a self is a fetter, they therefore assert that there is a self.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason does the self exist? Answer:
Because of right view.
The Buddha said:
"If a person sees that there is rebirth by transformation (upapāduka), they possess right view."
Because those various schools possess right view, there is therefore a self;
it is thus.
Furthermore, for what reason is there a self?
Answer: Because the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Buddha said:
One contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
If there were no self, these four objects of observation would not exist.
Since the various schools see that the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness, they conclude that the self exists.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason does the self exist? Answer:
Because the Buddha spoke of the śrāvakas,
the Buddha said:
"There are people who serve fire, burning their own bodies and encouraging others to burn themselves."
For this reason, the Buddha said that there is a person. Thus,
if there were no person, there would be no one to roast themselves, nor anyone else to roast.
Those various schools see that the Buddha spoke of a "person," and for this reason they perceive a self.
It is thus.
Furthermore, for what reason do those schools assert that there is a self?
Answer: Because when one person appears in the world, many people attain birth in peace and happiness.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
All those endowed with merit are born into this world so that many people may obtain peace and happiness.
If there were no person, who would produce such merit?
Since these various schools perceive that a single person is born, they therefore maintain that there is a self (*ātman*).
Thus it is. Furthermore, various schools maintain that the five aggregates (skandhas) are the person and the self.
It is asked:
Why is this? Answer: Because it is taught by way of the categories of elements (*dhātu*).
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"The six elements, the six sense bases, and the six types of contact constitute the person.

Because those various schools see that the Buddha taught that the six elements, the six sense bases, and the six types of contact constitute the person, they therefore maintain that this is the person.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason is this person not different from other persons? Answer:
Because the Buddha has spoken of sūtras such as the *Sūtra on the Most Excellent Woman* regarding foreign lands, the Buddha said:
"The 'most excellent woman' I speak of—whether she be white, black, blue, or smooth; whether square, long, short, slender-waisted, or stout—is simply a human being and nothing other than a human."
Thus it is. Furthermore, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there is a person who sees a certain bhikṣu as loathsome—whether he be short, or humpbacked, or lame."
Thus it is. Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"With my divine eye, I see sentient beings—those who are lovable, those who are hateful, and so forth."
It is so. Furthermore, it is said that those people in hell are like a stack of firewood being burned; the burning of the hell-beings is likewise thus.

Regarding what was previously stated concerning the most excellent women and others, as well as seeing monks who are loathsome—the Buddha sees sentient beings as either lovely or loathsome, even up to the burning of hell-beings like a stack of firewood—all these are merely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that constitute a person; there is no person other than this.
These various schools see that the Buddha taught the aggregates (*skandha*) are the person; therefore, they hold that the person is [identical to] them.
Furthermore, other schools maintain that the person is distinct from the five aggregates.
Why is this? Answer: Because they are like people carrying a heavy burden.
The Buddha said:
"The heavy burden is the five aggregates; the bearer is the person.
It is thus."
For this reason, the person and the aggregates are separate; for this reason, the person and the aggregates are distinct.
It is thus. Furthermore, for what reason is the person different from the aggregates?
The Buddha said:
"Do people take craving as their self?
Because they have transmigrated for a long time [in relation to it], therefore the person and craving are distinct."
For this reason, the person and the aggregates are distinct.
Furthermore, for what reason are the person and the aggregates distinct?
Answer: Because one experiences the fruit of karma.
The Buddha spoke this verse:
One rejoices in happiness in this life, and one rejoices with gladness in future lives;
performing merit brings joy in both places, as one sees for oneself the purity of one's karma.
When the retribution of karma in this world is exhausted, it must again be experienced in the next world.
When the aggregates (skandhas) perish, one proceeds according to karma to receive another distinct aggregate-body.
Because those various schools see that one receives karmic retribution, they hold that the person and the aggregates are separate.
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason are the person and the aggregates distinct? Answer:
Because I have said this, the Buddha spoke:
"In a previous life, I was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Sudarśana, also called Mahādeva; for this reason, I now receive a new aggregate (skandha), yet I am not different from my former self."
Therefore, the person and the aggregates are distinct.
Furthermore, for what reason are the person and the aggregates distinct?
Answer: Because it is taught in the context of the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The Buddha stated that the aggregates (skandha) are impermanent, but he did not state that the person (pudgala) is impermanent.

At times it is said that the aggregates (skandhas) possess the characteristic of impermanence, and at times it is said that the aggregates possess the characteristic of permanence; for this reason, the characteristic of permanence is distinct and the characteristic of impermanence is distinct. Therefore, the person and the aggregates are each thus distinct.
Furthermore, various schools assert that the person (*pudgala*) is eternal.
Why is this? Answer:
Because there is no fundamental basis, persons should not course within birth and death.
As the Buddha has said:
"Birth and death have no fundamental basis; sentient beings transmigrate, and the source and root of birth and death cannot be known."
Thus it is. Therefore, persons have no fundamental basis;
if a person has no fundamental basis, they likewise have no derivative end. Thus, the person is eternally such.
Furthermore, for what reason is the person eternal?
Answer: Because one recollects past lives.
The Buddha said:

"One recollects one lifetime, and even recollects births throughout incalculable eons of the past. Although the aggregates (skandhas) perish as one transmigrates through birth and death, the person does not perish.
Because those various schools see that one recollects one lifetime and even recollects births throughout incalculable eons of the past, they therefore hold that the person is eternal."
Thus it is.
Furthermore, for what reason is the person permanent? Answer:
Regarding the explanation of the locus,
the Buddha said:
"One who has crossed to the other shore and dwells on that ground is called a brāhmaṇa."
Thus it is.
The Buddha spoke again:
"Having already crossed to the other shore, one does not return again."
Thus it is.
The Buddha further said:
"Those who have crossed to the other shore abide there without falling back; having reached the other shore, they have no more sorrow or affliction."
It is so. If one sees a person who has crossed to the other shore and dwells there without falling back and without sorrow or affliction, therefore the person is eternal.
Because those various schools see that the Buddha spoke of such a state, they maintain that the person is eternal.
Furthermore, why is it that the person is eternal?
Answer: Because they reach the bliss of immovability.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Thus is right liberation; having crossed the muddy torrent of desire, the wise cannot fathom it, for they have attained the bliss of the immovable."
Because those various schools see that the Buddha taught [the self] reaches the bliss of immovability, they hold that the person is eternal.
Since this person reaches the bliss of immovability and is devoid of the aggregates (skandhas), this person’s location cannot be known; therefore, the person is eternal.
Thus it is. Furthermore, various schools assert that the person (*pudgala*) is impermanent.
Question:
Why is this? Answer: Because there is a fundamental cause.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“There is one person whose birth brings peace and happiness to all people in this way.
If there is birth, there is its root; if there is a root, there is its end.”
Therefore, it is thus that human beings are impermanent.
Furthermore, for what reason are human beings impermanent?
Answer: The Buddha spoke because he was addressing what is new.
The Buddha said:
The newly born devas possess a fine complexion, an upright appearance, and majestic virtue.
"New" refers to the dharma of impermanence; therefore, humans are impermanent.
It is thus.
Furthermore, for what reason is human existence impermanent?
Answer: Because it is a phenomenon of perversion.
The Buddha said:
"Although King Prasenajit is a ruler of men, in another world his state is thus inverted.
If there is an inverted dharma that constitutes impermanence, for this reason, humans are impermanent."
Furthermore, for what reason is human existence impermanent?
Answer: Because it is subject to falling away and arising.
Nirvāṇa is permanent; it neither falls away nor arises.
According to the Buddha’s teaching, I see that sentient beings fall away and arise; for this reason, based on the Buddha’s teaching of falling away and arising, people are impermanent.
Furthermore, for what reason are human beings impermanent?
Answer: Because they are subject to the laws of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The Buddha said:
"I am the spiritual friend for the countless members of the fourfold assembly. Because of birth and death, they come to me to attain liberation from birth and death.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are impermanent phenomena; therefore, human beings are impermanent."

Thus it is. Therefore, taking this sūtra as the basis, some say that there is no real self in such a manner; some say that it cannot be said whether a self exists in such a manner; and some say that a self exists in such a manner.
For this reason, we have given rise to doubt:

whether there truly exists a self, or whether it is merely a conventional designation. It is for this reason that some say the five aggregates are the self, some say the self is distinct from the five aggregates, some say it is permanent, and others say it is impermanent.
It is so. For this reason, we have conceived a doubt and ask:
How does a person abandon this existence and undergo another existence?

Answer: According to the intention of the Sūtras, through the power of teaching and transformation, it should be understood that the five aggregates of clinging constitute what is taken to be a real person.
Because the five aggregates of clinging constitute a person and are taken to be a real person, one cannot say that the person is either permanent or impermanent.
It is thus. An objection is raised:
In the preceding chapter, it was stated that "non-self" is primary, yet each [school] has its own attachments. How should this be explained so that they may attain understanding?
Answer: As previously stated, there is merely the arising of suffering; such is non-self.
We shall now explain this.
That which is suffering is suffering; arising and ceasing are the nature of suffering.
Desiring to reveal this nature of suffering, the Buddha spoke to Kātyāyana:
Suffering arises with arising; suffering ceases with cessation.
The arising and ceasing of the mark of self (ātman) cannot be expressed; therefore, the Buddha spoke thus.
Furthermore, as previously stated, because there is no discourse, there is no self.
It is so. We now speak thus, and we follow one another in faith and acceptance.
It is as the Buddha spoke to the non-Buddhists:
Although there is a self, it is a conventionally designated self; it is not a real self, for it is spoken of as a self based upon the contaminated aggregates (*āsravakṣaya-skandha*).
The Buddha, seeing the phenomena of the past and future, says that this is a self, but it is not a real self.
As the Buddha taught, one receives a name based on the performance of actions; therefore, the Buddha spoke of the designation "self.
It is thus. Furthermore, as previously stated, because one perceives it as one's own body, there is no self.
"So it is. We shall now speak. He replied:
Enveloped by ignorance, one regards the five aggregates—which are selfless—as a self.
It is like a newborn, ignorant infant who sees another woman and calls her his mother.
It is as the Buddha has taught: it is likewise that one regards the five aggregates, which are selfless, as being a self. It is so.
Furthermore, as previously stated, there is no self (*anātman*), because neither a self nor what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) can be apprehended.
It is thus; we shall now explain this further.
Answer: The Buddha taught that because [the self] is not independent, the true nature of "I" and "mine" cannot be found. It is so.
That which is constrained by another is not called self-constraint;
that which is self-constrained is not called constrained by another.
Therefore, one abandons both self-constraint and constraint by another, yet does not abandon the self.
So it is. Furthermore, as previously stated, because that which is unreal is said to exist, there is no self. So it is.
We now state: [The answer is] because they do not exist substantially.
That which is unreal does not correspond with non-existence; to speak of what does not exist as existing is a statement difficult to believe.
Therefore, one negates existence by speaking of non-existence, yet does not negate the self. Thus it is.
As previously stated by the various schools, because the characteristics [of a self] are inexpressible, it cannot be said whether a self exists or does not exist.
It is thus; we shall now explain this further.
It is said:
"The characteristics of permanence, impermanence, and so forth cannot be predicated [of it], but the existence of a self (ātman) and so forth can be predicated.
As the Buddha said:"
There are those who roast their own bodies and so forth, sacrificing everything.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"The unlearned and ignorant worldling takes evil karma as his characteristic; the wise person takes wholesome karma as his characteristic."
Therefore, the assertions of the various schools are not to be relied upon. It is so;
for as previously stated by those schools, regarding the questions of whether a self exists or does not exist, [the Buddha] remained silent and did not provide an answer.
It is so. We now explain that because [the question] is dissociated, it is set aside; because it is associated, it is not set aside.
As the Buddha has prophesied:
"The ignorant ordinary person is unwholesome; the wise person is wholesome.
Therefore, the words of the various schools (nikāyas) are not to be relied upon.

It is so. As stated previously by various schools, it is because the existence of a self and the non-existence of a self cannot be definitively described as being different from one another. It is so.
We shall now explain this.
If we were to examine it, would the agent be different from the action? It is so.
It should be explained whether this refers to the practice itself or to a practice distinct from it;
therefore, one should set aside the words of various schools as they are not to be relied upon. Thus it is.
As previously stated by the various schools, it is because the existence of a self and the non-existence of a self cannot be said to be either permanent or impermanent.
It is thus;
we now state this as well.
If the existence or non-existence of a self could be predicated, it would result in the views of nihilism or eternalism.
Relying on these two views is not permitted by the Buddha.
Furthermore, to say that there is no person at all would constitute a fault.
To say that such categories are indeterminate is incorrect. Why is this?
If one were to say that no person exists, that would be called a false view.
If one says that there is a person, this is called right view.
Therefore, it can be said that there is a person. As it is said in the Sūtra:
If one says there is no person, it is called false view; if one says there is a person, it is called the view of self.
If one says there is [a person], it is because that [person] would be either permanent or impermanent.
If it were so, then conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would be both permanent and impermanent.
If they were identical in their existence, then while conditioned phenomena are impermanent, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is permanent; but the person (*pudgala*) is not like this.
If there were both identity and difference as permanent, then impermanence should likewise be understood. It is thus:
as previously stated by various schools, it cannot be said whether there is a self or no self, because [the self] depends upon existence and non-existence.
It is so. We now say this: if there were no self at all, the Buddha should not have spoken of there being a basis.
Because the Buddha taught that there is a basis for dependence, it follows that a "self" can be spoken of;
it is thus. This is as previously stated by various schools: because there is the bondage of speech regarding a self.

It is so. We now declare that there is no person who can be bound, yet there is binding, just as in the case of a king’s prison bonds: though there is no person [therein], there is both binding and fettering. It is like having a rope and a knot, or lacking a rope and lacking a knot.
It is so. Although there is no self, there is the bondage of speech. It is so.
As has been stated by the various schools previously, because there is the right view that a self exists;
it is thus. We now state as follows.
Based on the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*), the Buddha speaks of a "person" (*pudgala*); because one perceives a person as having a person, this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
It is thus. This is as previously stated by various schools: that there is a self (*ātman*), because the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is so. We now speak thus.
The Buddha said to Kātyāyana:
It is mind-only; this is said in order to reveal the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
It is taught that it is mind-only, establishing that all dharmas are nothing other than this.
Thus it is.
Just as the various schools previously asserted that there is a self because the Buddha spoke of śrāvakas,
so too do we now assert this.
The Śrāvakas speak of the dharmas as the basis for their stations; it is merely the speech of the Śrāvakas and nothing more.
Just as the various schools previously asserted the existence of a self, they do so because of such assertions.
We now state this: the Buddha taught that there is a person who is a mere conventional designation;
therefore, their position is one of non-self.

If, in reality, there were no self, then killing would not be established; there would be neither a killer nor one who is killed. Likewise, there would be no stealing, sexual misconduct, or false speech; the same applies to drinking alcohol.

Thus, if there is no self, and if there is indeed no self, then even the five heinous crimes do not exist. One may indulge the sense faculties at will without giving rise to good or evil; there is neither bondage nor liberation. There is no binder, nor is there anything to be bound; there is no agent, nor is there karma or its retribution.
If karma does not exist, its retribution also does not exist.
If both karma and its retribution do not exist, there would likewise be no birth and death;
yet sentient beings revolve through birth and death by means of the retribution of their karma.
If there were no birth-and-death, the cause of birth-and-death would also not exist.
If there were no cause, the cessation of the cause would also not exist.
If the cessation of the cause did not exist, the path leading [to that cessation] would also not exist.
In this way, even the Four Noble Truths do not exist.
If the Four Noble Truths do not exist, then there is no Buddha who taught the Four Noble Truths.
If there is no Buddha, then there is also no Sangha.
In this way, if there were no person, the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths would also not exist.
Such various assertions are all untenable; for this reason, if there were no person, the aforementioned faults would ensue.
Furthermore, a subsequent fault also arises.
If there were someone who possessed a self (*ātman*), then the aforementioned faults would not apply.
As the Buddha taught in the sūtras, one should truly know this; therefore, a real self exists.
As has been stated by the various schools previously, the five aggregates constitute the person, as they are the gateway to the self and its elements.
It is thus; we now speak accordingly.
If someone were to ask me whether [the self] is different [from the aggregates], this sūtra does not reveal that there is a self.
Is the aggregate the self, or am I the aggregate?
If the aggregate were the self, then while the aggregate could be described, the self could not be described.
If the self were the aggregates, then the self could be described, whereas the aggregates cannot be so described.
Furthermore, both [positions] could be asserted: that the five aggregates are not the self. It is thus.
As previously stated by the various schools, the person is distinct from the five aggregates, because the person is like one who carries a heavy burden.
It is thus; we now state this.

It is in dependence upon the burden that one speaks of "having a burden. If the self were distinct from the aggregates, then when the aggregates perish or arise, the self would likewise arise or perish; and just as when a portion of the body is cut, the self would also have a corresponding portion.

In this way, one part becomes many parts, and many parts return to becoming one. When the body exists, life also exists; when life exists, the body also exists. Therefore, the aggregates (skandhas) are the self.
This statement may be refuted as follows: It is so,
for as previously stated by various schools, the person is distinct from the aggregates, because grasping and craving constitute two separate factors.
It is so. We now declare:
if a person possesses right view and is free from doubt, yet is bound by craving, they will revolve through birth and death.
The Buddha, wishing to reveal this, said:
"When people grasp at craving, it becomes their second [bond], causing them to dwell long in birth and death;
when craving is severed, there is no further transmigration."
Therefore, I am not different from the aggregates.
It is thus. As previously stated by other schools, the person and the aggregates are distinct, because the person experiences the fruits of karma.

It is so. We now declare that, based on the existence of outflow-tainted birth and death, one receives its retribution in this life and in future lives; therefore, the person and the aggregates are not distinct.
Furthermore, as has been stated by various schools previously—that the person and the aggregates are distinct—this is what I have taught.
It is thus; we now state it in this way.
Speaking according to the *pāramitās*,
the Buddha said:
"In the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I was once King Mūrdhaja."
Therefore, the person and the aggregates are not distinct.
Furthermore, as stated previously by other schools, the person and the aggregates are distinct, because [the Buddha] did not provide a definitive teaching on their location.

It is so. We now declare that it cannot be said whether the aggregates and the self are different or not different; therefore, the characteristics of phenomena—headed by permanence and impermanence—are inexpressible, and the self, too, is inexpressible.
If the self were distinct from the aggregates, the Buddha stated that whether the self is distinct from the body or not is among those things he did not declare;
it is not clarified in the sūtras. If the self were distinct from the aggregates, it would either have to exist within the aggregates or pervade all places.

If it were within the aggregates, then when the body is cut or when the body is broken, the self should be visible—just as when an *udumbara* fruit is broken, a mosquito inside it becomes visible; my being within the aggregates would be exactly like that.
If the self were distinct from the body, then when cold or heat touched the body, I would not perceive them.
Furthermore, if my eyes were plucked out, I should see objects even more clearly.
It is thus.
When the sense faculties perish, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth should likewise be perceived.
Furthermore, if the self were distinct from the body, it would pass from this body into that body, and then return again to enter this body.
It would be as if a person were to go from this house into that house, and then return again to this house;
such would be the case if the self were distinct [from the aggregates].
Furthermore, if the self were distinct from the aggregates, the self would not undergo birth in various places.
If one were to take birth in various places, one should take birth in all places simultaneously in a single moment;
therefore, it cannot be permanent, because it resides within the body.
Liberation is difficult to attain, and if one acts in various places, one should not engage in karmic activity.
If there were no karmic fruits and no meritorious deeds, and if there were neither bondage nor liberation, nor the practice of meditation, then one would already be liberated.
Such [consequences] are untenable; therefore, the person is distinct from the body, and this argument may be set aside.
Thus it is.
